html:
In April 1789, about fifteen months after the British colony at Sydney was founded, smallpox swept through the Aboriginal peoples around Port Jackson. With no immunity, they died in great numbers; perhaps around 70 percent of those infected died, and some clans were nearly wiped out.

Colonists found bodies on beaches and in rock shelters around the harbour. The Eora man Arabanoo, held captive by the British, nursed the sick and caught the disease himself. Almost no colonists fell ill.

Where it came from is still argued:

  • Some historians think it came from the First Fleet, which carried smallpox material in bottles for inoculation, by accident or on purpose.
  • Others think it came overland from the north, carried by Makassan visitors; see Makassan trepang trade.

The epidemic broke the Eora and their neighbours just as the colony began to spread, and made it easier for settlers to take the land. Survivors such as Bennelong became go betweens with the British. See also Smallpox in Sydney.
